blocks.content: 3.1 SEBI – Securities and Exchange Board of India

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: SEBI is the principal regulatory body overseeing the securities market and capital market functions in India.
BSE and NSE are the major stock exchanges facilitating secondary market transactions in India.
Capital market instruments primarily include equity shares, preference shares, debentures, and bonds.
Financial markets are broadly categorized into Primary Markets (for new security issues) and Secondary Markets (for trading existing securities).
The IPO (Initial Public Offering) process allows private companies to raise equity capital from public investors.

blocks.content: SEBI was established on April 12, 1988 as a non-statutory body and given statutory powers through the SEBI Act, 1992. Headquartered in Mumbai, it regulates the securities markets in India.

items: Protective Function – Prohibits insider trading, price rigging, fraudulent practices
Developmental Function – Promotes investor education, training of intermediaries
Regulatory Function – Registers and regulates brokers, merchant bankers, FIIs, mutual funds

items: SEBI received statutory status through the SEBI Act of 1992.
Distinction between Primary Market (new issues/IPOs) and Secondary Market (stock trading) is frequently asked in competitive exams.
BSE is Asia's oldest stock exchange (established in 1875), whereas NSE introduced nationwide screen-based electronic trading.
Fresh issuance of securities (IPO, FPO, Rights Issue); capital flows to issuer: Primary Market
Trading of existing securities on stock exchanges; capital flows between investors: Secondary Market
Short-term funds (< 1 year); RBI, banks, corporates; instruments: T-Bills, CP, CD, CBLO: Money Market
Long-term funds (> 1 year); equities and long-term bonds: Capital Market
Currency exchange; India has a managed float system; RBI intervenes when needed: Forex Market
